audio_caption: The audio clip begins with a male speaker, sounding educational, who mentions that he'd like his students to understand "the process involves vaporizing the liquid, then condensing the vapor back to a liquid, and collecting it." A second male speaker then adds that they'll "be using distillation extensively to remove solvent" and suggests that knowing the setup is important, so they'll go to stations to see how to do it "step by step." The clip then ends with a sound reminiscent of static or white noise.

The audio clip begins with a female speaker defining the boiling point of a liquid and discussing vapor pressure and its relationship to temperature, stating that boiling points are dependent on atmospheric pressure. She then provides an example of boiling eggs while hiking in the mountains.

The audio begins with a female speaker discussing the distillation process, noting how the temperature gradually increases to the boiling point. She continues with instructions to start from the bottom, choosing a heat source influenced by flammability and boiling point, and advises on using steam baths and heating mantles. She then mentions the chosen heat source in the demonstration is a Bunsen burner, because water has a high boiling point.

A female speaker explains the parts and function of a Bunsen burner, describing how to turn it on and adjust the flame, in an instructional tone. She then indicates the start of the assembly of a distillation apparatus.

The clip begins with a female speaker instructing on how to perform distillation, emphasizing the use of an iron ring and heat resistant gauze to prevent flask cracking when heated. The speaker describes how to clamp a round bottom flask, explains what flask size to use and why, and explains to add boiling stones. She then states to, "pour the liquid in using a funnel."

A female speaker begins with a methodical tone and directs the listener to "grease the lower joint of the still head three way adapter," clarifying that this helps prevent "freezing or sticking." She continues giving instructions on laboratory equipment assembly, including placing the joint in the "round bottom flask," greasing the thermometer adapter, positioning the thermometer bulb, and collecting distillate. She continues in the same instructional tone, detailing how to loosely clamp the receiving flask, lightly grease the condenser, and complete the assembly by inserting parts. She finishes by reminding listeners to "clamp your condenser using the metal joint clamps" and to note the location of all clamps.

The audio clip features a single female speaker in an instructional tone. She discusses the tendency of beginner students to over-clamp apparatus, explaining the potential consequences such as glassware breakage and stressing the importance of proper clamping techniques. She transitions to the distillation process, cautioning against heating a closed system and checking for an opening to equalize pressure, confirming that the described apparatus is not a sealed system or a bomb.

A female voice begins by giving instructions on starting distillation by adjusting water flow through the condenser, using a moderate flow rate, and explaining how increased pressure may cause rubber tubing to pop off. She continues to instruct on clamping the hoses to the condenser and water faucet, applying heat to gently boil the liquid, and observing the reflux ring. She further instructs on temperature readings, distillation rate, and liquid collection. The speaker emphasizes recording the temperature once it stabilizes. Finally, she instructs on cleaning the apparatus after distillation is completed. The female speaker has a clear, instructional tone. The clip ends with a brief review on assembling the apparatus to carry out the distillation of a liquid.
